title: Who owns the oceans?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss who owns the oceans, starting with Somali piracy off the Horn of Africa and the high seas being international waters. They trace the history of maritime law: the Freedom of the Seas doctrine and the three-mile territorial sea, the War of 1812 and World War I (Lusitania) as conflict flashpoints, Truman's 1945 unilateral extension of US waters (the "Great Sea Grab"), the rise in offshore oil and fishing, Arvid Pardo's call at the UN, and the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (proposed 1967, ratified 1982, in force 1994) which set territorial seas at twelve nautical miles, created exclusive economic zones out to 200 miles, and addressed landlocked nations' access. They also cover the Arctic resource race, straits, underwater hotels in Dubai and Fiji, the names of the five oceans, and listener mail.
topics: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea

segments.title: Opening banter and Somali pirates
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter and introduce modern Somali piracy, including ransom captures and the British Navy's confrontation with a pirate boat, and note that piracy off Africa has a long history.

segments.title: Pirates and the question of jurisdiction
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Somali pirates are hard to prosecute because no functioning central government exists and nobody clearly has jurisdiction. They say the high seas, including waters off Somalia, are international waters that belong to everyone, referencing the UN.

segments.title: Freedom of the Seas and the territorial sea
segments.summary: They trace early maritime law, from the Freedom of the Seas doctrine granting a three-mile buffer of exclusive waters off a coast to the modern territorial sea as an extension of national sovereignty.

segments.title: Wars over sea rights and the Great Sea Grab
segments.summary: The hosts describe how attacks in territorial and international waters contributed to the War of 1812 and World War I, then how Truman unilaterally extended US waters in 1945, with rising oil and fishing values driving the change.

segments.title: Overlapping claims and the UN convention
segments.summary: Other countries followed the US with overlapping 200-mile claims. Overfishing rose, and Arvid Pardo of Malta raised the issue at the UN in 1967, leading to the Convention on the Law of the Sea, ratified in 1982 and in force in 1994.
topics: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea

segments.title: Territorial seas, exclusive economic zones, straits, and the Arctic
segments.summary: The convention set the territorial sea at twelve nautical miles and created exclusive economic zones out to 200 miles. Straits narrower than the limit are treated as international water. The hosts describe the Arctic race for oil and gas under melting ice.

segments.title: Landlocked nations and underwater hotels
segments.summary: The hosts explain that landlocked countries have a right of access through coastal neighbors' waters without tariffs, yet suffer economically, citing the Central African Republic shipping costs. They then discuss underwater hotels in Dubai and Fiji and how leases on seabed land might work.

segments.title: Names of the five oceans
segments.summary: The hosts try to name the five oceans and settle on the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian, Arctic, and Southern Oceans.

segments.title: Listener mail and correction
segments.summary: A correction about rebreathers versus scuba buoyancy devices after a Niagara Falls episode, and a listener poem praising the show. The hosts plug the blog, website search, and email address.
